Data: [TidyTuesday 2026-09-15](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-09-15).

The Dead Sea Scrolls are often described as the oldest Bible we have.
That is true, and it leaves something out.
The people who kept these scrolls did not have a Bible in the sense of a closed list of books.
They had a library, and the catalogue of its 809 manuscripts shows what they copied, not what later tradition decided to keep.

The figure counts copies of each work.
A copy on papyrus, in the old Hebrew script, or in Greek still counts as a copy of its work, so every Exodus is an Exodus.
Deuteronomy and Psalms lead, with 29 certain copies each.
Isaiah follows with 18 and Genesis with 15.

Then comes Jubilees, with 14 certain copies.
It is a retelling of Genesis and the first part of Exodus, organised around a calendar of weeks of years, and it never entered the Hebrew Bible.
Exodus also has 14 certain copies.
A little further down, the Community Rule, the group's own rulebook, has 11 copies, which is as many as Leviticus.
1 Enoch has 10 certain copies, more than Daniel's 8.

So the red rows are not a fringe.
Six of the 14 works copied at least eight times sit outside the canon, and they sit in the middle of the list rather than at its foot.

Some cautions.
A manuscript here can be a whole scroll or a few scraps, and the catalogue counts both the same way.
What survived is what the caves happened to preserve, so a count is evidence of copying, not a measure of it.
The catalogue also files the odd copy inconsistently: one copy of Daniel is marked as outside the canon, so each work takes the status of most of its copies.
Outlined tiles are copies the editors mark with a question mark, and the counts leave them out; five of 1 Enoch's are fragments from Cave 7.
Phylacteries, mezuzot, and fragments that the catalogue cannot tie to one work are not drawn.
